title: Monitoring Models in Production: Drift, Data Quality and Alerts
subtitle: Catch broken pipelines, measure drift with statistics you build yourself, track performance when labels arrive late, and design alerts and retraining policies people trust.
outcomes: Design prediction logs and label tables, and catch pipeline incidents with data quality checks
Implement PSI, KS, chi-squared and Jensen-Shannon drift measures and know what each one misses
Measure performance on mature labels, estimate it before labels arrive, and detect concept drift
Learn alert thresholds from history, backtest alert rules and build a model-health dashboard
Choose and justify a retraining policy, accounting for label delay and feedback loops
prerequisites: Statistics for Data Science and AI (distributions and hypothesis tests) and Machine Learning Foundations with Python, or equivalent; Deploying and Serving Machine Learning Models helps for context. You need Python 3.10 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn and Matplotlib; no monitoring product is required.
description:
A model can keep answering requests long after its answers stop being good. This advanced course teaches you to notice: what to record when a model makes predictions, how to catch the pipeline bugs that cause most urgent incidents, and how to tell real changes in the world from noise. You'll build the core of a monitoring system yourself with NumPy and SciPy rather than a library whose API changes, so you know exactly what each number means: population stability index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-squared tests, Jensen-Shannon distance and a domain classifier.

The labs follow one fraud model through 20 simulated weeks with a unit bug, an outage, a new payment channel, rising amounts and a new fraud pattern. You'll see which signals catch which incident, why p-values mislead at production volumes, how to report performance honestly when labels arrive weeks late, how to estimate it in the meantime and where that estimate fails, and how to design alerts from backtests rather than rules of thumb. The course ends with retraining policies compared over a simulated year and a capstone that proves a monitoring system with incident drills.

modules.title: What to monitor, and the data to do it with
modules.summary: Record the prediction log and the labels that monitoring depends on, tell the kinds of drift apart, and catch broken pipelines with cheap data quality checks before any statistics run.

lessons.title: The prediction log: monitoring starts with records
objectives: Design a prediction log that supports every later monitoring question
Map service, data and model metrics to where each one comes from
key_points: Log every prediction with a unique ID, the time, the model version, the raw inputs as the model received them, the score and the decision; without that record, drift and performance can't be measured afterwards.
Keep labels in a separate table keyed by the same ID, with the date each label became known, and join the two when computing performance; labels arrive later and from other systems.

Service metrics (traffic, errors, latency) come from the server and its metrics stack; data metrics (missing values, ranges, categories, distributions) come from the log; model metrics (accuracy, calibration, business outcomes) need the labels.
Log inputs as the model saw them, after the feature pipeline, as well as the source values when you can: a bug between the two shows up only if both are recorded.
Prediction logs hold personal and sensitive data: apply the same access control, retention limits and minimisation as any other production data store.

lessons.title: Kinds of drift, and why labels arrive late
objectives: Distinguish covariate shift, prior shift and concept drift
Explain how label delay and feedback loops limit what can be measured
key_points: Covariate (data) drift is a change in the inputs' distribution P(X), such as larger payment amounts; prior shift is a change in how common each class is, P(Y); concept drift is a change in P(Y|X), the relationship the model learnt, such as a new fraud pattern.
Drift can be sudden (a pipeline change), gradual (inflation), recurring (seasons, paydays) or a one-off event; recurring patterns belong in the reference data, not in alerts.
Many apparent drifts are upstream changes rather than changes in the world: a unit switched from units to cents, a renamed category or a broken join. These need a pipeline fix, not a new model.
Labels often arrive late, as with fraud chargebacks after weeks or loan defaults after months, so the newest predictions can't be scored yet; input and prediction drift are the early warnings.

Feedback loops hide outcomes: a declined payment never shows whether it was fraud, so labels exist mostly for what the model let through. A small random sample handled without the model keeps an unbiased view.

lessons.title: Data quality checks that catch broken pipelines
objectives: Write data quality checks for a scored batch against a reference
Explain why quality checks run before drift statistics
key_points: Quality checks compare each new window with a reference period and with business rules: schema and types, missing-value rates, allowed ranges, known category sets, volume, duplicates and freshness.
They are cheap, need no labels and give a precise message, such as device_age_days 34.9% missing, which tells the on-call engineer where to look.
Drift statistics can be blind to quality failures: a test that drops missing values never sees a missing-value spike, and a unit bug that affects one channel can stay under a drift threshold.
Base limits on the business (an instant payment can't exceed the scheme limit) and on the reference (no more than 3% of values above the reference 99th percentile), and version them with the model.
Run quality checks first and treat failures as incidents in the data pipeline; compute drift only on data that passed, or the drift report becomes a second, noisier alarm for the same bug.

files.content:
"""Simulate 20 weeks of instant payments for a fraud model, with the incidents a real system meets.
Weeks 1-8 are the training period. From week 9 the model is live, and:
  week 12      a pipeline bug sends web amounts in cents (x100)
  week 14      an upstream outage leaves device_age_days empty for many rows
  weeks 15-20  a new channel, "wallet", appears
  weeks 16-20  amounts rise gradually (a real change: risk per payment stays the same,
               but the model, which scores on amount, drifts upwards)
  weeks 17-20  a new fraud pattern: small app payments from long-trusted devices (concept drift)
Fraud labels arrive late: a chargeback takes 3-40 days; a payment with none after 45 days counts as legitimate."""
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
START = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-05")          # a Monday
frames = []
for week in range(1, 21):
    n = int(rng.normal(3000, 120))
    channel_p = [0.45, 0.35, 0.20] if week < 15 else [0.40, 0.32, 0.18]
    channels = ["card", "app", "web"] if week < 15 else ["card", "app", "web", "wallet"]
    if week >= 15:
        channel_p = channel_p + [0.10]
    inflation = 1.0 + 0.06 * max(0, week - 15)               # weeks 16-20: up to +30%
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "ts": START + pd.to_timedelta(7 * (week - 1), "D") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.uniform(0, 7 * 86400, n), "s"),
        "amount": np.round(rng.lognormal(3.6, 0.9, n) * inflation, 2),
        "hour": rng.integers(0, 24, n),
        "channel": rng.choice(channels, n, p=channel_p),
        "device_age_days": rng.gamma(2.0, 120, n).round(0),
        "merchant_risk": np.round(rng.beta(2, 8, n), 3),
        "tx_last_1h": rng.poisson(0.8, n),
    })
    logit = (-6.4 + 0.6 * np.log(df.amount / inflation) + 1.6 * (df.hour < 5) + 1.0 * (df.channel == "web")
             - 0.007 * df.device_age_days + 6.0 * df.merchant_risk + 0.9 * df.tx_last_1h)
    if week >= 17:                                            # the new fraud pattern
        pattern = (df.channel == "app") & (df.amount < 40) & (df.device_age_days > 300)
        logit = logit + 4.0 * pattern
    df["is_fraud"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    if week == 12:                                            # pipeline bug: cents instead of units
        df.loc[df.channel == "web", "amount"] *= 100
    if week == 14:                                            # upstream outage
        df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.35, "device_age_days"] = np.nan
    df["week"] = week
    frames.append(df)

data = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True).sort_values("ts", ignore_index=True)
data.insert(0, "tx_id", [f"p{i:06d}" for i in range(len(data))])
delay = np.where(data.is_fraud == 1, rng.integers(3, 41, len(data)), 45)
data["label_known_at"] = (data.ts + pd.to_timedelta(delay, "D")).dt.floor("D")
Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
data.to_csv("data/payments.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote data/payments.csv: {len(data)} payments over 20 weeks, fraud rate {data.is_fraud.mean():.3f}")

"""Feature engineering shared by training and scoring, so both compute features the same way."""
import numpy as np

MODEL_FEATURES = ["log_amount", "night", "device_age_days", "merchant_risk", "tx_last_1h", "channel"]
RAW_FEATURES = ["amount", "hour", "channel", "device_age_days", "merchant_risk", "tx_last_1h"]


def add_features(df):
    out = df.copy()
    out["log_amount"] = np.log(out["amount"].clip(lower=0.01))
    out["night"] = (out["hour"] < 5).astype(int)
    return out

"""Train the fraud model on weeks 1-8, then write what a live system records: a prediction log with
the inputs, score and model version of every payment, and a separate table of labels as they arrive."""
import joblib
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

from features import MODEL_FEATURES, RAW_FEATURES, add_features

VERSION = "fraud-lr-2026.02"
data = add_features(pd.read_csv("data/payments.csv", parse_dates=["ts", "label_known_at"]))
train = data[data.week <= 8]

numeric = [f for f in MODEL_FEATURES if f != "channel"]
model = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), numeric),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["channel"]),
    ])),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
model.fit(train[MODEL_FEATURES], train.is_fraud)
joblib.dump(model, "fraud_model.joblib")

data["score"] = model.predict_proba(data[MODEL_FEATURES])[:, 1].round(6)
data["model_version"] = VERSION
log = data[["tx_id", "ts", "week", "model_version"] + RAW_FEATURES + ["score"]]
log.to_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", index=False)
data[["tx_id", "is_fraud", "label_known_at"]].to_csv("data/labels.csv", index=False)

print(f"trained {VERSION} on weeks 1-8: {len(train)} payments, "
      f"training AUC {roc_auc_score(train.is_fraud, model.predict_proba(train[MODEL_FEATURES])[:, 1]):.3f}")
print(f"wrote data/prediction_log.csv ({len(log)} rows) and data/labels.csv")

"""Data quality checks for each week of the prediction log, against the training weeks as reference.
They are cheap, need no labels, and catch broken pipelines before drift statistics are even computed."""
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
ref = log[log.week <= 8]
NUMERIC = ["amount", "hour", "device_age_days", "merchant_risk", "tx_last_1h"]
LIMITS = {"amount": (0.01, 10_000), "hour": (0, 23), "device_age_days": (0, 20_000),
          "merchant_risk": (0, 1), "tx_last_1h": (0, 500)}             # what the business allows
ref_weekly_rows = ref.groupby("week").size().mean()
ref_missing = ref[NUMERIC].isna().mean()
ref_p99 = ref[NUMERIC].quantile(0.99)
ref_channels = set(ref.channel.unique())


def check_week(df):
    problems = []
    rows = len(df)
    if abs(rows / ref_weekly_rows - 1) > 0.25:
        problems.append(f"volume {rows} rows vs about {ref_weekly_rows:.0f} expected")
    if df.tx_id.duplicated().any():
        problems.append(f"{df.tx_id.duplicated().sum()} duplicate tx_id values")
    for col in NUMERIC:
        missing = df[col].isna().mean()
        if missing > ref_missing[col] + 0.02:
            problems.append(f"{col}: {missing:.1%} missing (reference {ref_missing[col]:.1%})")
        low, high = LIMITS[col]
        outside = (~df[col].dropna().between(low, high)).sum()
        if outside:
            problems.append(f"{col}: {outside} values outside {low}-{high}")
        tail = (df[col] > ref_p99[col]).mean()
        if tail > 0.03:
            problems.append(f"{col}: {tail:.1%} above the reference 99th percentile (limit 3%)")
    new = set(df.channel.unique()) - ref_channels
    if new:
        counts = df.channel.value_counts()
        problems.append("channel: new values " + ", ".join(f"{c} ({counts[c]} rows)" for c in sorted(new)))
    return problems


for week, df in log[log.week >= 9].groupby("week"):
    problems = check_week(df)
    print(f"week {week:2}: " + ("ok" if not problems else "FAIL " + "; ".join(problems)))

hints: Week numbers in the output are padded to two characters, so week 9 prints as week  9.
If your numbers differ slightly, check the library versions; the incidents still show up in the same weeks.
A new category isn't automatically an incident: it may be a product launch the model has never seen, which is a reason to retrain rather than to fix a pipeline.

modules.title: Measuring drift with statistics
modules.summary: Implement PSI, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-squared tests and Jensen-Shannon distance yourself, learn what each one sees and misses, and why p-values mislead at production volumes.

lessons.title: The population stability index, done properly
objectives: Compute PSI with quantile bins and a guard for empty bins
Explain why the PSI rule of thumb is a convention, not a test
key_points: PSI = sum over bins of (a − e) × ln(a / e), where e and a are the shares of the reference and current data in each bin; it equals the KL divergence taken both ways, so it is symmetric.
Take bin edges from the reference's quantiles (deciles are common), with open-ended outer bins, so each bin holds about the same share of the reference and new extremes still land in a bin.
An empty bin makes ln(a / e) infinite, so implementations replace zero shares with a small epsilon; for a brand-new category, PSI is then dominated by that arbitrary epsilon.
The readings under 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate and over 0.25 major come from credit scoring practice; they aren't a statistical test, and in the lab a real unit bug scores 0.203.
PSI depends on the binning: more bins give larger values for the same data, so fix the binning per feature and compare like with like.

lessons.title: KS and chi-squared tests, and p-values at scale
objectives: Apply the two-sample KS test to numbers and the chi-squared test to categories
Prefer effect sizes to p-values when samples are large
key_points: The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic D is the largest gap between the two empirical cumulative distributions (scipy.stats.ks_2samp); it needs no bins and runs from 0 to 1.

For categories, scipy.stats.chi2_contingency tests a table of counts (reference and current by category), and Cramér's V = sqrt(chi² / (n × (min(rows, columns) − 1))) turns it into an effect size from 0 to 1.
With production volumes every difference becomes significant: in the lab, the same 0.05-standard-deviation shift gives p = 0.67 with 500 rows and p ≈ 1e-84 with 500,000, while D stays near 0.02.
Alert on effect sizes such as D, Cramér's V, PSI or Jensen-Shannon distance, with thresholds learnt from history, and use p-values only as a guard against reading noise in small windows.

Testing many features multiplies false alarms: at α = 0.05, 40 features with no drift give about two significant results per check; correct with Bonferroni (α / m) or Benjamini-Hochberg, or rank features by effect size.

lessons.title: Jensen-Shannon distance, and choosing a measure
objectives: Compute Jensen-Shannon distance and interpret its range
Choose a drift measure per feature type, including multivariate drift
key_points: Jensen-Shannon divergence averages the KL divergences of each distribution from their mixture M = (P + Q) / 2; it is symmetric and finite even with empty bins. scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon returns its square root, the JS distance, between 0 and 1 with base=2.

Wasserstein distance (scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance) measures how far values moved, in the feature's own units, which is easy to explain: week 20's amounts sit about 16 above the training weeks', while week 12's unit bug scores over 1,000.
Missing values are invisible to measures computed on the values that are present, so track the missing rate as its own metric, as the week 14 outage shows.

A domain classifier tests drift across all features together: train a model to tell reference rows from current rows; a cross-validated AUC near 0.5 means they look alike, and its feature importances point at what changed.
Weight drift by importance: a large shift in a feature the model barely uses matters less than a small one in its strongest feature, and drift in the score itself summarises what the model feels.

files.content:
"""Weekly drift report: each live week against the training weeks, feature by feature."""
import pandas as pd

from drift import chi2, js_distance, ks, psi, psi_categorical

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv")
ref = log[log.week <= 8]
rows = []
for week, cur in log[log.week >= 9].groupby("week"):
    row = {"week": week}
    for col in ["amount", "device_age_days", "score"]:
        d, p = ks(ref[col], cur[col])
        row[f"{col} psi"] = psi(ref[col], cur[col])
        row[f"{col} ks_d"] = d
        row[f"{col} js"] = js_distance(ref[col], cur[col])
    _, p_chan, v_chan = chi2(ref.channel, cur.channel)
    row["channel psi"] = psi_categorical(ref.channel, cur.channel)
    row["channel cramers_v"] = v_chan
    row["channel chi2_p"] = p_chan
    rows.append(row)

report = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("week")
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
print(report[["amount psi", "amount ks_d", "amount js", "device_age_days psi", "score psi",
              "channel psi", "channel cramers_v"]].round(3).to_string())
report.to_csv("drift_report.csv")
flagged = report[(report["amount psi"] > 0.25) | (report["score psi"] > 0.25) | (report["channel psi"] > 0.25)]
print("weeks over the 0.25 rule of thumb on amount, score or channel:", list(flagged.index))

"""The same small shift, tested with more and more data: the effect stays put, the p-value collapses."""
import numpy as np

from drift import ks, psi

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(f"{'rows':>8} {'KS D':>7} {'p-value':>10} {'PSI':>7}")
for n in [500, 5_000, 50_000, 500_000]:
    reference = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    current = rng.normal(0.05, 1.0, n)          # a shift of 5% of a standard deviation
    d, p = ks(reference, current)
    print(f"{n:>8} {d:>7.3f} {p:>10.2e} {psi(reference, current):>7.4f}")

"""PSI depends on how you bin: the same two samples, binned three ways."""
import pandas as pd

from drift import psi

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv")
ref, week20 = log[log.week <= 8].amount, log[log.week == 20].amount
for bins in (5, 10, 20, 50):
    print(f"amount PSI, week 20 vs reference, {bins:>2} quantile bins: {psi(ref, week20, bins):.3f}")

"""Multivariate drift: can a classifier tell reference rows from this week's rows? AUC near 0.5 means no."""
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv")
features = ["amount", "hour", "device_age_days", "merchant_risk", "tx_last_1h"]
ref = log[log.week <= 8].sample(6000, random_state=0)
for week in (10, 12, 18, 20):
    cur = log[log.week == week]
    X = pd.concat([ref[features], cur[features]])
    y = [0] * len(ref) + [1] * len(cur)
    auc = cross_val_score(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=100, random_state=0), X, y,
                          cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"week {week}: domain classifier AUC {auc:.3f}")

hints: If the channel PSI looks absurd, work it out by hand for the wallet bin: (0.10 − 0.0001) × ln(0.10 / 0.0001) is about 0.69 on its own.
domain_classifier.py runs five-fold cross-validation four times and can take a minute.
Weeks 17-20 show amount drift without any quality failure: that's the gradual rise in amounts, a real change rather than a bug.

modules.title: Performance when labels arrive late
modules.summary: Measure performance only on windows whose labels have matured, estimate it from calibrated scores in the meantime, and detect concept drift in the stream of errors once labels arrive.

lessons.title: Measuring performance on mature labels
objectives: Compute performance by window as known on a given date
Recognise the bias of scoring windows whose labels are incomplete
key_points: Join the prediction log to the labels by ID and compute metrics by prediction window (such as the week a payment was scored), not by the week the label arrived.
A window is mature when every label it can get has arrived: with chargebacks in 3 to 40 days and payments treated as legitimate after 45, a week is mature 45 days after it ends.
Scoring an immature window is biased: the labels known early are mostly the positives, so in the lab week 20's precision from known labels is 1.000, from 14 labelled payments, all fraud.
Report the label coverage beside every metric, and show immature windows as pending rather than as a number.
Weekly metrics on a few hundred positives are noisy, so compare against the spread seen in stable weeks, or add bootstrap confidence intervals, before calling a change real.

lessons.title: Estimating performance before labels arrive
objectives: Estimate precision and recall from calibrated probabilities
State the assumptions that make the estimate fail
key_points: If the model is calibrated, the expected number of frauds among flagged payments is the sum of their probabilities, so estimated precision = mean score of flagged payments, and estimated recall = flagged scores' sum ÷ all scores' sum.
This is confidence-based performance estimation (CBPE), the idea behind tools such as NannyML; it gives a figure for this week, weeks before the labels do.
It assumes the model is still calibrated and that P(Y|X) hasn't changed: covariate shift is fine, but concept drift isn't, and broken inputs aren't either.

In the lab, the estimate stays near 0.50 while realised precision falls to about 0.42-0.46 after the new fraud pattern appears, and week 12's broken amounts produce an estimate of 0.626 against a real 0.305.
Treat the estimate as an early indicator alongside prediction drift, and confirm with realised metrics as each window matures.

lessons.title: Detecting concept drift in the error stream
objectives: Run a Page-Hinkley test on a stream of errors
Trade detection delay against false alarms
key_points: Once labels mature, a sequential test on an error measure, such as the daily Brier score (mean squared difference between probability and outcome), detects when errors move up and stay up.
Page-Hinkley keeps the running mean and a cumulative sum of (value − mean − δ); it alarms when the sum rises more than λ above its lowest point, then resets to learn the new normal.

δ sets the size of change to ignore and λ the evidence needed: a smaller λ detects sooner but raises more false alarms. In the lab, λ = 0.03 detects the new fraud pattern in week 18 and λ = 0.05 only in week 20.
CUSUM works in a similar way; both are cheap enough to run on every model, but they see only labelled windows, so the label delay adds to the detection delay.
An alarm says errors rose, not why: check data quality and drift for the same period before concluding it's concept drift.

lab.title: Estimate performance without labels, then check it

"""Performance by week, as known on a given date. Fraud labels arrive over 3-40 days and a payment
counts as legitimate only after 45 days, so recent weeks can't be scored yet. Until they can, the
model's own probabilities give an estimate (confidence-based performance estimation)."""
import argparse

import pandas as pd

THRESHOLD = 0.3                       # payments scoring at least this go to manual review

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--as-of", default="2026-05-25", help="the date you run the report (end of week 20)")
args = parser.parse_args()
as_of = pd.Timestamp(args.as_of)

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
labels = pd.read_csv("data/labels.csv", parse_dates=["label_known_at"])
data = log.merge(labels, on="tx_id")
data["known"] = data.label_known_at <= as_of

print(f"as of {as_of.date()}, threshold {THRESHOLD}")
print(f"{'week':>4} {'labelled':>9} {'est prec':>9} {'real prec':>10} {'est recall':>11} {'real recall':>12}")
for week, g in data[data.week >= 9].groupby("week"):
    flagged = g.score >= THRESHOLD
    # Expected frauds among flagged rows = sum of their probabilities (valid if the model is calibrated).
    est_precision = g.score[flagged].mean()
    est_recall = g.score[flagged].sum() / g.score.sum()
    coverage = g.known.mean()
    if coverage == 1.0:
        tp = (flagged & (g.is_fraud == 1)).sum()
        real_p, real_r = f"{tp / flagged.sum():.3f}", f"{tp / g.is_fraud.sum():.3f}"
    else:
        real_p = real_r = "immature"
    print(f"{week:>4} {coverage:>9.0%} {est_precision:>9.3f} {real_p:>10} {est_recall:>11.3f} {real_r:>12}")

latest = data[data.week == 20]
seen = latest[latest.known]
naive = (seen.is_fraud[seen.score >= THRESHOLD] == 1).mean()
print(f"week 20 precision from the labels known so far: {naive:.3f} "
      f"({len(seen)} of {len(latest)} labelled, {seen.is_fraud.mean():.0%} of them fraud)")

"""Page-Hinkley change detection on the daily Brier score (mean squared error of the probabilities),
once labels have matured. It alarms when errors rise above their running mean and stay there."""
import argparse

import pandas as pd


class PageHinkley:
    def __init__(self, delta=0.002, threshold=0.03, min_days=7):
        self.delta, self.threshold, self.min_days = delta, threshold, min_days
        self.reset()

    def reset(self):
        self.n, self.mean, self.cum, self.min_cum = 0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0

    def update(self, x):
        """Feed one value; True means the mean has shifted upwards."""
        self.n += 1
        self.mean += (x - self.mean) / self.n
        self.cum += x - self.mean - self.delta       # delta: changes smaller than this are ignored
        self.min_cum = min(self.min_cum, self.cum)
        return self.n >= self.min_days and self.cum - self.min_cum > self.threshold


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--delta", type=float, default=0.002)
parser.add_argument("--threshold", type=float, default=0.03)
args = parser.parse_args()

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
labels = pd.read_csv("data/labels.csv")
data = log.merge(labels, on="tx_id")
data = data[data.week >= 9]
data["day"] = data.ts.dt.floor("D")
data["brier"] = (data.score - data.is_fraud) ** 2
daily = data.groupby("day").agg(brier=("brier", "mean"), week=("week", "first"))

detector = PageHinkley(delta=args.delta, threshold=args.threshold)
for day, row in daily.iterrows():
    if detector.update(row.brier):
        print(f"alarm on {day.date()} (week {int(row.week)}): daily Brier {row.brier:.4f}, "
              f"running mean {detector.mean:.4f}")
        detector.reset()                              # start learning the new normal
print(f"days monitored: {len(daily)}, mean daily Brier {daily.brier.mean():.4f}")

modules.title: Alerts and dashboards people trust
modules.summary: Learn thresholds from history, backtest alert rules before they page anyone, build a model-health dashboard, and investigate an alert with a runbook.

lessons.title: Designing alerts: thresholds, persistence and severity
objectives: Learn alert thresholds from a metric's behaviour in a stable period
Backtest alert rules for false alarms and detection delay
key_points: Learn each threshold from history: compute the metric on many windows from a stable period (leaving each window out of its own reference) and alert above a high quantile, such as the 99th percentile plus a margin.
Thresholds differ by feature, metric and window size, because noise does: a daily window of 400 payments wobbles more than a weekly one of 3,000.
Persistence, such as two windows in a row, cuts alerts from one-off blips at the cost of a window's delay; in the lab it removes one of week 12's seven alert days.

Backtest before going live: replay months of windows and count alerts on quiet periods and the delay on known incidents; in the lab the fixed 0.25 rule catches 2 of 7 bug days and none of the drift days.
Give alerts severities and owners: page only for what needs action now, such as a broken pipeline, send slower drift to a ticket queue, and attach a runbook link to each one.

lessons.title: Dashboards for model health
objectives: Lay out a model-health dashboard by monitoring layer
Show performance honestly when labels are late
key_points: Organise the dashboard by layer, top to bottom: service (volume, errors, latency), data quality, drift, then model performance, so a reader can follow a problem from symptom to cause.
Plot drift against the thresholds the alerts actually use, and mark deployments, retrains and known incidents on the time axis.
Show estimated performance and realised performance side by side, with realised values only for mature windows; a line that silently stops is easy to misread.
Prefer few, decision-oriented panels to many: each should answer a question someone acts on, such as whether the review queue's precision is falling.
Export monitoring metrics to the team's observability stack, such as Prometheus gauges graphed in Grafana; the course Observability with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry covers that machinery.

lessons.title: Investigating an alert
objectives: Follow a runbook from an alert to a decision
Choose between fixing data, retraining, rolling back and adjusting a threshold
key_points: Start with data quality for the same window: many urgent model alerts trace back to a pipeline, schema or upstream change, and those need a data fix, not a new model.
Then localise: which features, segments and channels moved, whether the score distribution moved, and whether the timing matches a deployment or a business event.
Decide on evidence: a pipeline bug is fixed and the bad predictions rescored; real drift that hurts performance leads to retraining; a model release that broke things is rolled back.
Some alerts are expected, such as a known campaign or a seasonal peak: record why, and if they recur, add the pattern to the reference instead of muting the alert.
Write up each incident briefly (signal, cause, action, time to detect and resolve) and feed the lessons back into checks, thresholds and runbooks.

"""Backtest alert rules on daily windows. A rule earns trust by staying quiet on normal days and
firing early on real incidents, so compare a fixed rule of thumb with thresholds learnt from history."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from drift import psi

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
log["day"] = log.ts.dt.floor("D")
ref = log[log.week <= 8]
METRICS = ["amount", "score"]


def daily_psi(frame, reference):
    return {m: psi(reference[m], frame[m]) for m in METRICS}


# 1. What does each metric look like on normal days? Leave each reference day out in turn.
history = []
for day, frame in ref.groupby("day"):
    history.append(daily_psi(frame, ref[ref.day != day]))
history = pd.DataFrame(history)
learnt = history.quantile(0.99) * 1.2            # a high quantile of normal days, plus a margin
print("learnt thresholds:", {m: round(v, 3) for m, v in learnt.items()},
      f"(from {len(history)} reference days; max seen {history.max().round(3).to_dict()})")

# 2. Score every live day, then apply three rules.
live = []
for day, frame in log[log.week >= 9].groupby("day"):
    live.append({"day": day, "week": int(frame.week.iloc[0]), "rows": len(frame), **daily_psi(frame, ref)})
live = pd.DataFrame(live)
over_learnt = live[METRICS].gt(learnt).any(axis=1)
rules = {
    "fixed PSI > 0.25": live[METRICS].gt(0.25).any(axis=1),
    "learnt threshold": over_learnt,
    "learnt, 2 days running": over_learnt & over_learnt.shift(1, fill_value=False),
}
quiet = live.week.isin([9, 10, 11, 13])          # weeks with no incident in the simulation
print(f"\n{'rule':24} {'quiet days alerted':>19} {'week 12 bug':>12} {'weeks 16-20 drift':>18} {'first alert':>12}")
for name, fired in rules.items():
    first = live.day[fired].min()
    first = str(first.date()) if pd.notna(first) else "-"
    print(f"{name:24} {int((fired & quiet).sum()):>11} of {int(quiet.sum()):<5} "
          f"{int((fired & (live.week == 12)).sum()):>6} of 7 "
          f"{int((fired & live.week.between(16, 20)).sum()):>11} of 35 {first:>12}")
live.to_csv("daily_metrics.csv", index=False)

"""A one-page model-health dashboard: volume, data quality, drift against learnt thresholds, and
performance as far as labels allow. Run alerts.py first: it writes daily_metrics.csv."""
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")                    # draw to a file, no window needed
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("data/prediction_log.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
log["day"] = log.ts.dt.floor("D")
labels = pd.read_csv("data/labels.csv", parse_dates=["label_known_at"])
daily = pd.read_csv("daily_metrics.csv", parse_dates=["day"])
as_of = pd.Timestamp("2026-05-25")

per_day = log.groupby("day").agg(rows=("tx_id", "size"),
                                 missing=("device_age_days", lambda s: s.isna().mean()),
                                 new_channel=("channel", lambda s: (s == "wallet").mean()))
joined = log.merge(labels, on="tx_id")
weekly = joined[joined.score >= 0.3].groupby("week").agg(estimated=("score", "mean"), real=("is_fraud", "mean"))
mature = joined.groupby("week").label_known_at.max() <= as_of

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(10, 11), sharex=False)
axes[0].plot(per_day.index, per_day.rows)
axes[0].set_title("Service: payments scored per day")
axes[1].plot(per_day.index, per_day.missing, label="device_age_days missing")
axes[1].plot(per_day.index, per_day.new_channel, label="share of unseen channel 'wallet'")
axes[1].set_title("Data quality")
axes[1].legend()
for metric in ("amount", "score"):
    axes[2].plot(daily.day, daily[metric], label=f"{metric} PSI vs training weeks")
axes[2].axhline(0.25, linestyle="--", color="grey", label="0.25 rule of thumb")
axes[2].set_title("Drift (daily PSI)")
axes[2].legend()
axes[3].plot(weekly.index, weekly.estimated, marker="o", label="estimated precision (from scores)")
axes[3].plot(weekly.index[mature], weekly.real[mature], marker="s", label="realised precision (mature labels)")
axes[3].set_title(f"Model: precision of review queue, labels as of {as_of.date()}")
axes[3].set_xlabel("week")
axes[3].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("monitoring_dashboard.png", dpi=110)
print(f"saved monitoring_dashboard.png: {len(fig.axes)} panels, {len(per_day)} days, "
      f"{int(mature.sum())} weeks with mature labels")

modules.title: Retraining triggers and closing the loop
modules.summary: Choose when to retrain, retrain safely on the right window, and keep feedback loops and the monitoring system itself under watch.

lessons.title: When to retrain: schedules and triggers
objectives: Compare scheduled, drift-triggered and performance-triggered retraining
Explain how label delay limits each trigger
key_points: Scheduled retraining (such as every eight weeks) is simple and predictable and keeps up with gradual change; it can retrain when nothing changed or wait too long after a sudden change.

Drift-triggered retraining reacts to input or score drift, but drift isn't damage: harmless shifts can trigger it, and concept drift that leaves the inputs alone never will, as the lab's simulation shows.
Performance-triggered retraining reacts to measured damage, but only after labels mature, so it is always at least the label delay behind, and weekly metrics are noisy enough to trigger by chance.
Combine them: a schedule as the backstop, performance triggers for damage, drift and quality signals for investigation, and a cool-down period so one problem doesn't cause a burst of retrains.
Never retrain on data that failed quality checks: a model trained on the week of the unit bug learns the bug.

lessons.title: Retraining safely
objectives: Choose a training window for a retrain
Hand a retrained model over to evaluation and release
key_points: The training window trades recency for stability: a short recent window adapts quickly but is noisy and forgets seasons; a long one is stable but slow; weighting recent data is a middle way.
Only matured labels can be used, so a retrain at week w with a four-week label delay trains on data up to week w − 4 at best.
Evaluate the retrained model on the newest matured data it didn't train on, against the current champion on the same data and segments, before anything is promoted.

Hand over through the same release path as any model: registry, gate, then shadow or canary, as in the courses MLOps Foundations: Experiments, Models and Reproducibility with MLflow and Deploying and Serving Machine Learning Models.
Reset the monitoring reference after a release: drift is measured against the new model's training data, and its first windows set the new baseline.

lessons.title: Feedback loops and monitoring the monitor
objectives: Recognise feedback loops that bias labels and retraining data
Monitor the monitoring system itself
key_points: A model's decisions change its future data: declined payments never get outcome labels, and reviewed ones get better labels than the rest, so retraining data over-represents what the model let through.
A small holdout handled without the model, or with random exploration, gives unbiased labels to measure the model and retrain on; its cost is part of the monitoring budget.
Fraudsters adapt to the model itself, so in adversarial settings expect concept drift after every release, and watch the segments the model newly lets through.
Monitor the monitoring: alert when a drift job doesn't run, when the prediction log stops growing or when labels stop arriving, because a silent monitor looks exactly like a healthy model.
Review the system periodically: retire alerts nobody acts on, check thresholds against new history, and confirm each runbook still matches the pipeline.

files.content:
"""A year of weekly payments in which fraud slowly changes shape, and labels arrive four weeks late.
Four retraining policies face the same data; each retrain uses the latest eight weeks of labels."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

from drift import psi

WEEKS, LAG, WINDOW, COOL_DOWN = 52, 4, 8, 4
FEATURES = ["merchant_risk", "tx_last_1h", "night", "log_amount", "new_device"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)


def make_week(week, n=2000):
    t = max(0, week - 8) / 44                       # 0 up to week 8, rising to 1 by week 52
    X = pd.DataFrame({
        "merchant_risk": rng.beta(2, 8, n),
        "tx_last_1h": rng.poisson(0.8, n),
        "night": (rng.integers(0, 24, n) < 5).astype(int),
        "log_amount": rng.normal(3.6 + 0.3 * t, 0.9, n),       # amounts drift up: harmless
        "new_device": (rng.random(n) < 0.15).astype(int),
    })
    logit = (-4.5 + 0.7 * t + (6.0 - 6.0 * t) * X.merchant_risk + 0.9 * X.tx_last_1h
             + 1.6 * X.night + 0.3 * (X.log_amount - 0.3 * t) + (0.3 + 3.2 * t) * X.new_device)
    return X, (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)


DATA = {w: make_week(w) for w in range(1, WEEKS + 1)}


def train(weeks):
    X = pd.concat([DATA[w][0] for w in weeks])
    y = np.concatenate([DATA[w][1] for w in weeks])
    model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
    return model, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]


def run(policy):
    model, train_scores = train(range(1, 9))
    baseline_auc, last_retrain, retrains, aucs = None, 8, [], {}
    for week in range(9, WEEKS + 1):
        X, y = DATA[week]
        scores = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        aucs[week] = roc_auc_score(y, scores)        # the truth, for scoring the policy only
        matured = week - LAG                          # the newest week whose labels are known
        due = False
        if policy == "every 8 weeks":
            due = (week - 8) % 8 == 0
        elif policy == "on score drift" and week - last_retrain >= COOL_DOWN:
            due = psi(train_scores, scores) > 0.1
        elif policy == "on performance" and week - last_retrain >= COOL_DOWN and matured > last_retrain:
            Xm, ym = DATA[matured]
            observed = roc_auc_score(ym, model.predict_proba(Xm)[:, 1])
            baseline_auc = observed if baseline_auc is None else baseline_auc
            due = observed < baseline_auc - 0.02
        if due:
            model, train_scores = train(range(matured - WINDOW + 1, matured + 1))
            baseline_auc, last_retrain = None, week
            retrains.append(week)
    return retrains, aucs


print(f"{'policy':16} {'retrains':>8} {'mean AUC wk 9-52':>17} {'mean AUC wk 45-52':>18}  retrained in weeks")
for policy in ["never", "every 8 weeks", "on score drift", "on performance"]:
    retrains, aucs = run(policy)
    auc = pd.Series(aucs)
    print(f"{policy:16} {len(retrains):>8} {auc.mean():>17.3f} {auc.loc[45:].mean():>18.3f}  {retrains}")

hints: The simulation draws all 52 weeks once, before any policy runs, so every policy faces exactly the same data.
AUC here is computed with true labels for scoring the policies only; the policies themselves see labels only after LAG weeks.
A single noisy week can set a high baseline for the performance trigger: averaging two or three mature weeks makes it steadier.

project.title: A monitoring system for a payment-fraud model
project.brief: The fraud team's model scores every instant payment, and the last incident went unnoticed for three weeks. Build the monitoring system that would have caught it. Starting from the course's simulator (run it with a new seed, or adapt it), design the prediction log and label table; write data quality checks; compute drift with at least three measures, with thresholds learnt from history and backtested; report performance on mature labels with an estimate for immature weeks; detect degradation in the error stream; and draw a dashboard. Then prove it works with incident drills: inject at least four incidents of different kinds (such as a unit bug, missing data, a new category, gradual covariate drift and concept drift) into a fresh simulation, and report which signals caught each one, and how quickly. Finish with a retraining policy, supported by a simulation, and a runbook for the on-call engineer.
